Motives of melonic graphs

Paolo Aluffi, Matilde Marcolli, and Waleed Qaisar Address: Florida State University, Tallahassee
USA Email address: aluffi@math.fsu.edu Address: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena
USA
University of Toronto, Toronto
Canada
Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, Waterloo
Canada Email address: matilde@caltech.edu Address: University of Toronto, Toronto
Canada Email address: waleed.qaisar@mail.utoronto.ca
Abstract.

We investigate recursive relations for the Grothendieck classes of the affine graph hypersurface complements of melonic graphs. We compute these classes explicitly for several families of melonic graphs, focusing on the case of graphs with valence-44 internal vertices, relevant to CTKT tensor models. The results hint at a complex and interesting structure, in terms of divisibility relations or nontrivial relations between classes of graphs in different families. Using the recursive relations we prove that the Grothendieck classes of all melonic graphs are positive as polynomials in the class of the moduli space ℳ0,4\mathcal{M}_{0,4}. We also conjecture that the corresponding polynomials are log-concave, on the basis of hundreds of explicit computations.

1. Introduction

In this paper we obtain a recursive formula for the Grothendieck classes (virtual motives) of the graph hypersurfaces associated to the melon-tadpole graphs. This provides a recursively constructed family of mixed-Tate motives, which includes the motives associated to the leading melonic terms of certain bosonic tensor models.

Our motivation in considering the behavior of the motives of melon and melon-tadpole graphs comes from the fact that several interesting physical models are dominated in the large NN limit by melonic graphs. This is the case for SYK models (see [13] for a rigorous diagrammatic proof), as well as in group field theory (see for instance [7]) and tensor models ([12], [16], [21], [23]), which include generalizations of the SYK models (see for instance [18], [31]).

1.1. Graph polynomials and CTKT models

The graph polynomials that one expects to find, when representing amplitudes in Feynman parametric form in the setting of group field theory and tensor models, are usually of the form described in [19] or [30]. The Tanasa graph polynomials of [30] are generalizations of the Bollobás-Riordan polynomial that satisfy the deletion-contraction relation. Similarly, the Gurau polynomials of [19] also satisfy a deletion-contraction relation. The motives of hypersurfaces associated to these polynomials may be, in principle, amenable to the kind of algebro-geometric techniques discussed in [4], which we rely on in this paper, but in a form more similar to the case of the Potts models we analyzed in [5]. However, the computation of the Grothendieck class we obtain here relies essentially on the recursive form of the Grothendieck class for splitting an edge and for replacing an edge by a number of parallel edges, obtained in [4]. These formulas do not have a simple counterpart for the case of the Potts models and other graph polynomials with deletion-contraction. This means that a more general computation of the polynomials of [19] or [30] probably requires a much more thorough analysis and would not be an immediate generalization of the argument presented here. Other parametric realizations of tensor models, such as [17], do not even satisfy a deletion-contraction relation, hence they cannot be addressed via the method of [4] and of this paper.

The case we focus on here, however, is simpler and it involves the usual graph hypersurfaces associated to the Kirchhoff–Symanzik polynomial of the graph, for a massless scalar theory. These are relevant to tensor models in the case of the melonic sector of the CTKT models. We briefly recall below the setting used in [9] that motivates the computations we present in this paper. The case of the graph polynomials of [19] or [30] will be left to a future investigation. Note that, if a similar argument can be applied to such polynomials, or to the massive melonic graphs, one does not expect to obtain a family of motives with the mixed-Tate property, since it is known that already for small graphs in such families the mixed-Tate property fails, [10], [28]. Thus, the mixed-Tate property is certainly specific to the case of the massless Kirchhoff–Symanzik polynomial.

When one computes the contributions to the expansion at leading order in 1/N1/N and all orders in the coupling constants, this is usually done using the 44-colored graphs expansion of tensor models ([11], [20], [22]) with 33-colored graphs for the different interaction terms as mentioned above (bubbles) and another color for the propagators connecting these 33-colored bubbles. However, as shown in [9], it is possible to also consider an expansion in ordinary Feynman graphs, which are obtained by shrinking all the bubbles to points. The free energy of the model is written in [9] in the form of a sum over connected vacuum 44-colored graphs with labelled tensor vertices,

with nt​(G)n_{t}(G), np​(G)n_{p}(G), and nd​(G)n_{d}(G) the number of tetrahedral, pillow, and double-trace bubbles, respectively, and F⁡(G)F(G) the number of faces and with 𝔸⁡(G){\mathbb{A}}(G) the amplitude of GG written in terms of edge propagators (see §2.1 of [9]). One then replaces the 44-colored graphs GG in this expansion with ordinary Feynman graphs by first replacing all the pillow and double trace bubbles with their minimal resolution in terms of tetrahedral bubbles (as in Figure 3 of [9]). An ordinary Feynman graph is then obtained by replacing these bubble by vertices. The resulting graph corresponds to a term of order zero in 1/N1/N iff it is a melon-tadpole graph, that is, a graph obtained by iterated insertion of melons or tadpoles into a melon or tadpole (Figure 2). In the absence of pillows and double traces one would obtain just melonic graphs. The amplitudes 𝔸⁡(G){\mathbb{A}}(G) of the resulting ordinary melon-tadpole Feynman graphs can then be computed in the Feynman parametric form, in terms of the Kirchhoff–Symanzik polynomial, as in [9]. We will not discuss here the renormalization problem for the resulting Feynman integrals, for which we refer the reader to [9]. We focus here instead on the algebro-geometric and motivic properties of these melon-tadpole Feynman integrals.

From the point of view of motivic structures in quantum field theory (see [27] for a general overview), our goal here is to show that massless CTKT models are dominated by a recursively constructed family of mixed-Tate motives.

1.3. Families of melonic graphs

The melonic and melon-tadpole graphs that occur in the massless CTKT models are all constrained by the condition that all vertices have valence 44, because of the form (1.1) of the action functional. In order to study the recursive properties of the Grothendieck classes associated to these graphs, however, it is convenient to consider them as a subfamily of a larger family of graphs, which include melonic graphs with vertices of arbitrary valences.

Moreover, in the typical description of melonic graphs, one assumes that the melonic insertions are separated by edge propagators (equivalently, one performs an insertion by first splitting an edge into three edges by the insertion of two valence-two vertices and then replaced the middle edge by a number of parallel edges). Again, in our setting it is more convenient to consider these graphs as a subfamily of a larger family of melonic graphs where an edge can be split into a number of subedges and each of them replaced by a set of parallel edges. The typical case of graphs with only valence-four internal vertices and including edge propagators will guide us in the choice of the examples illustrating the main recursive construction.

We also consider graphs with external edges and graphs (vacuum bubbles) without any external edges. Instead of following the usual physics convention of regarding external edges as half-edges (flags), we consider then as edges with a valence-one vertex. In this setting, when considering non-vacuum graphs for the CTKT case, we will allow formal valence-one vertices (to mark the external edges) in addition to the valence-four vertices of the self-coupling interactions.

We will not treat separately the melon-tadpole graphs. Indeed our more general class of graphs includes the operation of bisecting an edge with an intermediate vertex and a melon-tadpole graph is simply obtained by grafting together at the vertex two melonic graphs with this operation performed on one of their edges. Since the Grothendieck classes for graphs joined at a vertex is just a product, these classes are easily derived from the ones in the family we work with.

1.4. Summary of the paper

In §2 we present a convenient formalism for the recursive construction of melonic graphs with arbitrary valences and we show that a subclass of “reduced constructions” always suffices. We reformulate the construction in terms of labelled bipartite rooted trees. We then focus on the main case of interest for CTKT models, where graphs have all (internal) vertices of valence four.

In §3 we recall some basic facts about the Grothendieck ring of varieties, the parametric Feynman integrals, the graph hypersurfaces defined by the Kirchhoff–Symanzik polynomial, and the Grothendieck classes of the affine graph hypersurface complement. We focus on the Grothendieck class because it is universal among invariants which behave well with respect to basic set-theoretic operations. For example, the Grothendieck class determines the Hodge–Deligne numbers of the complement of the (affine) graph hypersurface, as well as the number of points of the complement over finite fields. We obtain a recursive formula for the Grothendieck class of melonic graphs with arbitrary valences. This formula can be effectively implemented in a standard symbolic manipulation system, and is also useful as a tool to study general features of Grothendieck classes of melonic graphs. For example, we prove that the Grothendieck class of a melonic graph can be expressed as a polynomial with positive coefficients in the class 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} of the moduli space ℳ0,4\mathcal{M}_{0,4}, i.e., 𝕊=[ℙ1∖{0,1,∞}]{\mathbb{S}}=[{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\}]. Extensive computer evidence also suggests the following:

Conjecture.

The polynomial expressing the Grothendieck class of a melonic graph is log-concave (in the sense of [29]).

It is well known (see [24]) that the log-concavity property often reflects some deeper underlying geometric structure, in the form of some kind of Hodge–de Rham relations. It seems likely that log-concavity of these Grothendieck classes as functions of 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} may indeed be pointing to some richer geometric structure.

In §4 we focus on the case of melonic graphs with (internal) vertices of valence four, and we consider particular recursive subfamilies, for which explicit generating functions can be obtained, both for vacuum bubbles and for graphs with external edges, with an explicit relations between these two cases. The generating functions in these cases and in the others considered in the paper were first obtained by carrying out explicit computations using the recursive formula obtained in §3. As an example of the type of result we obtain, consider the family consisting of graphs Γn\Gamma_{n} of the form

with nn interlocked circles. Let Pn​(u,v)P_{n}(u,v) be the Hodge–Deligne polynomial of the complement ZnZ_{n} of the affine graph hypersurface determined by Γn\Gamma_{n}. That is, Pn​(u,v)=∑ep,q​up​vqP_{n}(u,v)=\sum e^{p,q}u^{p}v^{q}, where ep,q=∑k(−1)k​hp,q​(Hck​(Zn))e^{p,q}=\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}h^{p,q}(H^{k}_{c}(Z_{n})) (see e.g., [15]). As a consequence of Proposition 4.1, the following holds:

Pn​(u,v)=(u​v−1)n​(u​v)2​n+1⋅An​(u​v−1),P_{n}(u,v)=(uv-1)^{n}(uv)^{2n+1}\cdot A_{n}(uv-1)\quad,

where the polynomial An​(t)A_{n}(t) is determined by the equality of formal power series ∑n≥0An​(t)​rn=∑k≥0ak​(r,t)\sum_{n\geq 0}A_{n}(t)r^{n}=\sum_{k\geq 0}a_{k}(r,t), with

∑k≥0ak​(r,t)​skk!=er​s​cos⁡((r2−r​t)12​s).\sum_{k\geq 0}a_{k}(r,t)\frac{s^{k}}{k!}=e^{rs}\cos((r^{2}-rt)^{\frac{1}{2}}s)\quad.

Alternative expressions for An​(t)A_{n}(t) are given in §5; in fact, the information carried by the polynomials An​(t)A_{n}(t) may be encoded in a rational generating function.

In §5 we analyze from the same viewpoint extensions of these recursive subfamilies to the more general case of arbitrary valences. Again we obtain that the corresponding Grothendieck classes are determined by rational generating functions.

In §6 we focus on the melonic vacuum bubbles, and we establish a general relation between their Grothendieck classes and those of associated non-vacuum graphs. We describe a procedure for studying the structure of valence-four melonic vacuum bubbles in terms of their tree structure, and we identify certain families of recursive relations, in the form of “melonic vacuum stars”.

In §7 we give rigorous proofs of all the statements presented in the previous sections.

2. Melonic graphs

2.1. The construction of melonic graphs

A graph with two vertices and nn parallel edges connecting them is variously referred to in the literature as a melon graph, a banana graph, or a sunset graph. In the spirit of botanical egalitarianism, we will use the “banana” terminology when referring to these basic building blocks, and call “melonic” the result of iterating the operation of replacing edges of a graph by strings of bananas. (We call this operation the ‘bananification’ of the edge.)

Thus, the basic iterative operation constructing melonic graphs is the following:

We allow arbitrary sizes a1,…,ara_{1},\dots,a_{r} for the banana components. Edges ought to be directed in order to determine the order of inclusion of the bananas; in fact this will be done implicitly in what follows, since it does not affect the invariant (Grothendieck class) we are computing. A melonic graph is obtained by applying this operation to an initial single edge, then applying it iteratively to any edge of the resulting graphs.

We can refer to the initial edge as the graph obtained ‘at stage 00’; the application of the iterative process at any stage may be encoded by a tuple

((a1,…,ar),p,k)((a_{1},\dots,a_{r}),p,k)

to represent the replacement of one single edge in the kk-th banana constructed at stage pp.

The motivation behind these requirements should be evident from the interpretation discussed above. For example, (v) expresses the constraint that the jj-th banana constructed at stage ii has enough edges to accommodate later replacements.

Definition 2.2.

A melonic graph is a graph determined by a melonic construction by the procedure explained above. ⌟\lrcorner

Every melonic construction determines a melonic graph up to graph isomorphism. Of course different melonic constructions may determine the same melonic graph. We say that two constructions T′T^{\prime}, T′′T^{\prime\prime} are ‘equivalent’ if the resulting graphs are isomorphic.

2.2. Reduced melonic constructions

Constructions such as Example 2.2 suggest the following definition.

Definition 2.3.

We say that a construction is reduced if it does not prescribe the replacement of the edge of a 11-banana past stage 00. ⌟\lrcorner

Formally, this requirement prescribes that

  • (vi)

    For all ti=((a1,…​ari),pi,ki)t_{i}=((a_{1},\dots a_{r_{i}}),p_{i},k_{i}), i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n: If aj=1a_{j}=1, then ks≠jk_{s}\neq j for all ss such that ps=ip_{s}=i.

The process illustrated above—replacing 11-bananas by their descendants—may be performed on every melonic construction, and produces an equivalent reduced construction. Therefore:

Lemma 2.1.

Every melonic graph admits a reduced construction.

Reduced constructions suffice in order to define melonic graphs, but it is important to consider non-reduced constructions as well; these may appear in intermediate steps of the recursive computation we will obtain in §3.

2.3. Melonic graphs and bipartite rooted trees

There is a convenient way to visualize a melonic construction as a labeled bipartite tree. Each tuple ((a1,…,ar),p,k)((a_{1},\dots,a_{r}),p,k) may be viewed as a rooted tree

with (black) leaves labeled by the integers aia_{i}. The (white) root will be attached to the kk-th leaf of the pp-th tree; this grafting procedure builds a rooted tree encoding the same information as a melonic construction. Item (v) in Definition 2.1 amounts to the requirement that the valence of a (black) node labeled aa be at most a+1a+1; that is, at most aa ‘descending’ edges can be adjacent to such a vertex.

The tree corresponding to a melonic construction has one white node for each tuple in the construction; thus, the depth of the melonic construction equals the number of white nodes in the corresponding tree.

Example 2.3.

The rooted trees corresponding to the two melonic constructions in Example 2.2 are

As noted in Example 2.2, these non-isomorphic labeled trees determine isomorphic melonic graphs. ⌟\lrcorner

The ‘reduced’ condition (vi) is the requirement that nodes labeled 11 necessarily be leaves. Every tree can be reduced (cf. Lemma 2.1) by ‘sliding up’ trees grafted at nodes labeled 11, as the case encountered in Example 2.1 illustrates.

We also note that the melonic graphs determined in Definition 2.2 have arbitrary vertex valences, while in a specific physical theory the valences are constrained by the terms in the action. The additional generality is needed for the recursion formula we will obtain in §3; we will choose families of graphs with fixed valence in most of the examples illustrating the recursion in §4, 5, and 6.

2.4. Valence-four melonic graphs

We will be especially interested in the case in which the valence of all internal vertices of the melonic graph is 44. The corresponding melonic constructions consist of tuples of the type

We will also consider the ‘vacuum’ flavor of these constructions, in which the two external vertices are identified; for example

Definition 2.4.

A vacuum melonic graph is a melonic graph without valence-11 vertices. ⌟\lrcorner

Vacuum melonic graph in which every vertex has valence 44 may be obtained by iteratively applying the basic bananification ((1,3,1),ps,ks)((1,3,1),p_{s},k_{s}) starting from a 44-banana. For example, the string of circles depicted above is produced by the construction

while the construction

Note that all vacuum valence-44 melonic graphs may also be constructed by starting from a 22-banana, performing iteratively the basic (1,3,1)(1,3,1) bananifications, and then removing the two extra valence-22 vertices produced at the beginning. Indeed, the 44-banana itself admits such a description: the melonic construction

(((2),0,1),((1,3,1),1,1))(((2),0,1),((1,3,1),1,1))

produces the 44-banana graph wth two extra valence-22 vertices on one of the edges. This alternative will be convenient in our computations concerning certain families of vacuum melonic graphs in §6.

3. Grothendieck classes of melonic graphs

3.1. The Grothendieck ring of varieties

For 𝒱𝕂{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathbb{K}} the category of varieties over a field 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} (which we can here assume to be 𝕂=ℚ{\mathbb{K}}={\mathbb{Q}}), the Grothendieck group of varieties K0​(𝒱𝕂)K_{0}({\mathcal{V}}_{\mathbb{K}}) is the abelian group generated by isomorphism classes [X][X] of varieties X∈𝒱𝕂X\in{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathbb{K}} with the inclusion-exclusion relation

[X]=[Y]+[X∖Y][X]=[Y]+[X\smallsetminus Y]

for closed subvarieties Y⊂XY\subset X. This group may be given a ring structure by defining [X]⋅[Y]=[X×Y][X]\cdot[Y]=[X\times Y] and extending by linearity. Grothendieck classes, sometimes referred to as virtual motives, behave like a universal Euler characteristic for algebraic varieties. Grothendieck classes usually provide more computable information about the nature of the motive of a variety. In particular, a Grothendieck class is Tate if it is contained in the subring generated by the Lefschetz motive 𝕃=[𝔸1]{\mathbb{L}}=[{\mathbb{A}}^{1}] (the class of an affine line), or equivalently in the ring generated by 𝕋:=𝕃−1{\mathbb{T}}:={\mathbb{L}}-1. Since the formulas we will obtain will naturally be polynomials in this class, and we will also be interested in expressing them in terms of the class 𝕊:=𝕃−2{\mathbb{S}}:={\mathbb{L}}-2, we highlight their definitions.

Definition 3.1.

We will denote by 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} the class of the ‘torus’ in the Grothendieck ring of varieties, i.e., 𝕋=[𝔸1∖𝔸0]=𝕃−1∈K0​(𝒱𝕂){\mathbb{T}}=[{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus{\mathbb{A}}^{0}]={\mathbb{L}}-1\in K_{0}({\mathcal{V}}_{\mathbb{K}}). We will also denote by 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} the class of the complement of three points in ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}: 𝕊=[ℙ1∖{0,1,∞}]=𝕋−1{\mathbb{S}}=[{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\}]={\mathbb{T}}-1. ⌟\lrcorner

Varieties whose motive is in the category of mixed Tate motives will have a Tate Grothendieck class. The converse holds conditionally (see [6] for a discussion of this point).

3.2. Kirchhoff–Symanzik polynomials

We consider the Kirchhoff–Symanzik polynomial of a graph GG with nn edges

(3.1) ΨG​(t)=∑T⊂G∏e∉E⁡(T)te,\Psi_{G}(t)=\sum_{T\subset G}\prod_{e\notin E(T)}t_{e},

as a polynomial in variables t=(t1,…,tn)t=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}) associated to the edges of GG, with the sum taken over all the spanning trees of the graph. This is a homogeneous polynomial of degree ℓ=b1​(G)\ell=b_{1}(G), the number of loops of GG. Thus, we can consider the associated projective graph hypersurface

(3.2) XG={t=(t1:⋯:tn)∈ℙn−1|ΨG(t)=0}.X_{G}=\{t=(t_{1}:\cdots:t_{n})\in{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}\,|\,\Psi_{G}(t)=0\}.

Up to renormalization of divergences, the Feynman parameter form of the Feynman integral for the graph GG, for a massless scalar field theory, is of the form

(3.3) U(G,p)=Γ⁡(n−D​ℓ/2)(4​π)ℓ​D/2∫ΔnVG​(t,p)−n+ℓ​D/2ΨG​(t)D/2dt1⋯dtnU(G,p)=\frac{\Gamma(n-D\ell/2)}{(4\pi)^{\ell D/2}}\int_{\Delta_{n}}\frac{V_{G}(t,p)^{-n+\ell D/2}}{\Psi_{G}(t)^{D/2}}dt_{1}\cdots dt_{n}

as a function of the external momenta pp, with VG​(t,p)V_{G}(t,p) the second Symanzik polynomial (defined in terms of cut sets of GG), DD the spacetime dimension, and the integration performed on the nn-simplex. In particular (modulo divergences) the Feynman integral (3.3) can be regarded as the integration of an algebraic differential form on a locus defined by algebraic equations (that is, a period) on the complement of the hypersurface XGX_{G}, hence the interest in investigating the nature of the motive of ℙn−1∖XG{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}\smallsetminus X_{G} through the computation of its Grothendieck class. For a general introductory survey of parametric Feynman integrals and their relations to periods and motives of graph hypersurfaces see [27].

In the following we will consider both graphs with external edges and graphs (vacuum bubbles) with no external edges. From the point of view of the parametric Feynman integral, the contribution of the external edges with their assigned external momenta is encoded only in the second Symanzik polynomial VG​(t,p)V_{G}(t,p), while the variables t=(te)t=(t_{e}) run over internal edges. Thus, as long as the exponent satisfies ℓ​D/2≥n\ell D/2\geq n, with ℓ\ell the number of loops, nn the number of (internal) edges, and DD the spacetime dimension, the Feynman integral is computed on the complement of the graph hypersurface defined by Kirchhoff–Symanzik polynomial ΨG​(t)\Psi_{G}(t) that only depends on the internal edges of GG. The Grothendieck class of the affine complement of the hypersurface of a graph GG (including external edges) and of the same graph with the external edges removed are simply related by a product by a power of 𝕃{\mathbb{L}} (the class of the affine line), hence it is equivalent to compute one or the other. For the purpose of computing Grothendieck classes, considering all graphs (both vacuum bubbles and non-vacuum graphs) for a massless scalar theory with a self-interaction term of order NN, so that the corresponding Feynman graphs have (internal) vertices of valence NN, is equivalent to considering all vacuum bubble graphs for a massless scalar theory with self-interaction terms of orders v≤Nv\leq N. We will work for convenience with graphs with the external edges included.

Up to the issue of renormalization, the Feynman integral (3.3) can then be seen as a period of the graph hypersurface complement. The nature of the motive of the graph hypersurface complement (detected by its Grothendieck class) then provides information on the kind of numbers that can be obtained as periods. The regularization and renormalization of the integral (3.3) can also be dealt with geometrically in terms of blowups or deformations. We will not discuss this in the present paper and we refer the reader to [27] for an overview and to the references therein for more information.

3.3. Grothendieck classes of graph hypersurface complements

In previous work, especially [3] and [4], we have focused on the essentially equivalent information given by the complement of the affine cone X^G\hat{X}_{G} in its ambient affine space, and studied its class in the Grothendieck group of varieties (the ‘motivic Feynman rule’ of [3]). For short, we will refer to this class as the Grothendieck class of the graph or of the corresponding melonic construction.

Definition 3.2.

The Grothendieck class of GG (or of any of its melonic constructions) is the class 𝕌⁡(G)=[𝔸n∖X^G]∈K0​(𝒱𝕂){\mathbb{U}}(G)=[{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus\hat{X}_{G}]\in K_{0}({\mathcal{V}}_{\mathbb{K}}) of the complement of X^G\hat{X}_{G} in its natural ambient affine space 𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n}, with nn the number of edges of GG. ⌟\lrcorner

By construction, 𝕌⁡(G){\mathbb{U}}(G) is the class of a variety of dimension equal to the number of edges of GG.

In this section we will use the melonic constructions introduced in §2 to obtain a recursive computation of the Grothendieck class of a melonic graph. The class only depends on the isomorphism class of the resulting graph, so equivalent constructions produce the same Grothendieck class.

We recall the following properties of 𝕌⁡(G){\mathbb{U}}(G).

  • •

    This invariant is ‘multiplicative’, in the sense that

    𝕌⁡(Γ1∪Γ2)=𝕌⁡(Γ1)⋅𝕌⁡(Γ2){\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{1}\cup\Gamma_{2})={\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{1})\cdot{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{2})

    if Γ1,Γ2\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2} are graphs joined at one vertex (or disjoint);

  • •

    For Γ=\Gamma=a loop, 𝕌⁡(Γ)=𝕋{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma)={\mathbb{T}} (with 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} as in Definition 3.1);

  • •

    For Γ=\Gamma=a single edge, 𝕌⁡(Γ)=𝕃=𝕋+1{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma)={\mathbb{L}}={\mathbb{T}}+1;

  • •

    If Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} is obtained from Γ\Gamma by splitting an edge, then 𝕌⁡(Γ′)=(𝕋+1)⋅𝕌⁡(Γ){\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{\prime})=({\mathbb{T}}+1)\cdot{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma);

  • •

    If Γ\Gamma is an mm-banana, m>0m>0, then

    (3.4) 𝕌⁡(Γ)=𝔹m:=m​𝕋m−1+𝕋⋅𝕋m−(−1)m𝕋+1{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma)={\mathbb{B}}_{m}:=m{\mathbb{T}}^{m-1}+{\mathbb{T}}\cdot\frac{{\mathbb{T}}^{m}-(-1)^{m}}{{\mathbb{T}}+1}

    ([2] and [4, Corollary 5.6]);

  • •

    More generally: if ee is not a bridge or a looping edge, then for suitable polynomials fmf_{m}, gmg_{m}, hmh_{m} in 𝕋{\mathbb{T}},

    (3.5) 𝕌⁡(Γm​e)=fm​𝕌​(Γ)+gm​𝕌​(Γ/e)+hm​𝕌​(Γ∖e),{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{me})=f_{m}{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma)+g_{m}{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma/e)+h_{m}{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma\smallsetminus e)\quad,

    where:

    • –

      Γm​e\Gamma_{me} stands for the graph obtained from Γ\Gamma by replacing ee with mm parallel edges joining the same vertices as ee;

    • –

      Γ∖e=Γ0​e\Gamma\smallsetminus e=\Gamma_{0e} is Γ\Gamma with ee deleted; and

    • –

      Γ/e\Gamma/e is Γ\Gamma with ee contracted.

    This is a weak form of a deletion-contraction relation. Inductively, the coefficients fm,gm,hmf_{m},g_{m},h_{m} are determined by their value for m≤2m\leq 2; in fact, we have

    (3.6) fm=𝕋m−(−1)m𝕋+1,gm=m​𝕋m−1−𝕋m−(−1)m𝕋+1,hm=𝕋m+(−1)m​𝕋𝕋+1f_{m}=\frac{{\mathbb{T}}^{m}-(-1)^{m}}{{\mathbb{T}}+1},\quad g_{m}=m{\mathbb{T}}^{m-1}-\frac{{\mathbb{T}}^{m}-(-1)^{m}}{{\mathbb{T}}+1},\quad h_{m}=\frac{{\mathbb{T}}^{m}+(-1)^{m}{\mathbb{T}}}{{\mathbb{T}}+1}

    as obtained in [4, Corollary 5.7]. Formulas for bridges and looping edges are easier, as they follow immediately from the multiplicativity property.

3.4. Recursion formulas for the Grothendieck classes

The properties listed above, and particularly identity (3.5), lead to recursion formulas for the computation of the Grothendieck class of the melonic graph associated with a melonic construction, or equivalently of the corresponding tree. (We will use the two descriptions interchangeably.) We will abuse language and use both 𝕌⁡(T){\mathbb{U}}(T) and 𝕌⁡(G){\mathbb{U}}(G) for the Grothendieck class of the melonic graph GG resulting from a melonic construction TT.

The recursion formulas are based on the following observations.

Let GG be a melonic graph given by a melonic construction (tree) TT.

  • •

    By Lemma 2.1, we may assume that the melonic construction is reduced, i.e., nodes labeled 11 are leaves of the tree TT.

  • •

    If TT has depth 11, i.e., the corresponding melonic construction consists of a single tuple ((a1,…,ar),0,1)((a_{1},\dots,a_{r}),0,1), then

    𝕌⁡(T)=∏i=1r𝔹ai=∏i=1r(ai​𝕋ai−1+𝕋​𝕋ai−(−1)ai𝕋+1).{\mathbb{U}}(T)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}{\mathbb{B}}_{a_{i}}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\left(a_{i}{\mathbb{T}}^{a_{i}-1}+{\mathbb{T}}\frac{{\mathbb{T}}^{a_{i}}-(-1)^{a_{i}}}{{\mathbb{T}}+1}\right)\quad.

Indeed, the graph GG consists of a string of bananas in this case.

If T=(t1,…,tn)T=(t_{1},\dots,t_{n}) has higher depth, consider the last state tnt_{n}. By construction, the black nodes of tnt_{n} are all leaves of TT.

  • •

    If tn=((a),p,k)t_{n}=((a),p,k), then an equivalent tree of depth n−1n-1 is obtained by omitting tnt_{n} and increasing the label of the kk-th leaf of tpt_{p} by a−1a-1.

    Indeed, this step of the construction simply replaces 11 edge in the kk-th banana of tpt_{p} by aa parallel edges.

  • •

    If tn=((1,…,1⏟r times),p,k)t_{n}=((\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{\text{$r$ times}}),p,k), then let T′=(t1,…,tn−1)T^{\prime}=(t_{1},\dots,t_{n-1}) be the construction obtained by omitting the last stage. Then 𝕌⁡(T)=(𝕋+1)r−1​𝕌​(T′){\mathbb{U}}(T)=({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{r-1}{\mathbb{U}}(T^{\prime}). Indeed, the effect of tnt_{n} is to split one edge in the kk-th banana of tpt_{p} a total of r−1r-1 times.

  • •

    We may therefore assume that tn=((a1,…,ar),p,k)t_{n}=((a_{1},\dots,a_{r}),p,k) with r>1r>1 and such that am=max⁡(a1,…,ar)>1a_{m}=\max(a_{1},\dots,a_{r})>1. The effect of tnt_{n} is to replace one edge in the kk-th banana of tpt_{p} by a string of a1,…,am,…,ara_{1},\dots,a_{m},\dots,a_{r}-bananas; this is the same as replacing that edge by a string of a1,…,am−1,1,am+1,…,ara_{1},\dots,a_{m-1},1,a_{m+1},\dots,a_{r}-bananas, and then replacing the resulting single edge ee by ama_{m} parallel edges.

    Let G′G^{\prime} be the graph obtained from GG by replacing the ama_{m}-banana by the single edge ee. With notation as in (3.5), we have G=Gam​e′G=G^{\prime}_{a_{m}e}.

    Claim 3.1.

    The edge ee is not a bridge (or a looping edge) of G′G^{\prime}.

    Proof.

    This follows from the assumption that TT be reduced. Indeed, as a consequence the kk-th banana of tpt_{p} does not consist of a single edge; hence removing one edge of this banana does not disconnect the graph. Since the edge ee is one edge in a subdivision of one edge of the kk-th banana of tpt_{p}, removing it does not disconnect the graph. (And the construction never produces looping edges, therefore ee is not a looping edge.) ∎

    +(am​𝕋am−1−𝕋am−(−1)am𝕋+1)​𝕌​(T′′)\displaystyle+\left(a_{m}{\mathbb{T}}^{a_{m}-1}-\frac{{\mathbb{T}}^{a_{m}}-(-1)^{a_{m}}}{{\mathbb{T}}+1}\right){\mathbb{U}}(T^{\prime\prime})

Corollary 3.3.

The graph hypersurface of a melonic graph GG determines a mixed Tate motive; the Grothendieck class 𝕌⁡(G){\mathbb{U}}(G) is a polynomial in 𝕃{\mathbb{L}} of degree equal to the number of edges of GG.

Proof.

The recursion implies immediately that 𝕌⁡(G){\mathbb{U}}(G) is a polynomial in 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}, therefore in 𝕃=𝕋+1{\mathbb{L}}={\mathbb{T}}+1. By construction, 𝕌⁡(G){\mathbb{U}}(G) is the class in the Grothendieck group of a variety of dimension equal to the number of edges of GG, so the statement follows. ∎

3.5. Positivity and log-concavity

The class of a melonic graph can of course also be written as a polynomial in the class 𝕊=𝕋−1=[ℙ1∖{0,1,∞}]{\mathbb{S}}={\mathbb{T}}-1=[{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\}]. Remarkably, these polynomials are ‘positive’, in the following sense.

Corollary 3.4.

Let GG be a melonic graph. Then 𝕌⁡(G)=P⁡(𝕊){\mathbb{U}}(G)=P({\mathbb{S}}) for a polynomial P⁡(t)=an​tn+⋯+a1​t+a0∈ℤ⁡[t]P(t)=a_{n}t^{n}+\cdots+a_{1}t+a_{0}\in{\mathbb{Z}}[t] with nonnegative integer coefficients.

Proof.

Given the recursion, it suffices to observe that the classes of banana graphs, 𝔹m​(𝕋)=𝔹m​(𝕊+1){\mathbb{B}}_{m}({\mathbb{T}})={\mathbb{B}}_{m}({\mathbb{S}}+1), and the coefficients fm,gm,hmf_{m},g_{m},h_{m} are all positive as polynomials in 𝕊{\mathbb{S}}. The key observation is the following.

Claim 3.5.

The class

𝕋m−(−1)m𝕋+1=(𝕊+1)m−(−1)m𝕊+2\frac{{\mathbb{T}}^{m}-(-1)^{m}}{{\mathbb{T}}+1}=\frac{({\mathbb{S}}+1)^{m}-(-1)^{m}}{{\mathbb{S}}+2}

is positive in 𝕊{\mathbb{S}}; in fact,

𝕋m−(−1)m𝕋+1=∑j=1m−1∑i=1m2(m−2​ij−1)𝕊j+{0if m is even1if m is odd.\frac{{\mathbb{T}}^{m}-(-1)^{m}}{{\mathbb{T}}+1}=\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\sum_{i=1}^{\frac{m}{2}}\binom{m-2i}{j-1}\,{\mathbb{S}}^{j}+\left\{\begin{aligned} 0&\quad\text{if $m$ is even}\\ 1&\quad\text{if $m$ is odd}\end{aligned}\right.\quad.

This is a straightforward computation, left to the reader. Given Claim 3.5, it follows immediately that

𝔹m=m​𝕋m−1+𝕋​𝕋m−(−1)m𝕋+1,fm=𝕋m−(−1)m𝕋+1,hm=𝕋m+(−1)m​𝕋𝕋+1{\mathbb{B}}_{m}=m{\mathbb{T}}^{m-1}+{\mathbb{T}}\frac{{\mathbb{T}}^{m}-(-1)^{m}}{{\mathbb{T}}+1}\quad,\quad f_{m}=\frac{{\mathbb{T}}^{m}-(-1)^{m}}{{\mathbb{T}}+1}\quad,\quad h_{m}=\frac{{\mathbb{T}}^{m}+(-1)^{m}{\mathbb{T}}}{{\mathbb{T}}+1}

are positive in 𝕊{\mathbb{S}}. As for

the required positivity follows from the fact that for all m,i≥1,jm,i\geq 1,j

which is clear, as (m−1j)=(m−2j−1)+(m−2j)≥(m−2j−1)≥(m−2​ij−1)\binom{m-1}{j}=\binom{m-2}{j-1}+\binom{m-2}{j}\geq\binom{m-2}{j-1}\geq\binom{m-2i}{j-1} for i≥1i\geq 1. ∎

Example 3.1.

The melon-tadpole graph of Figure 2 consists of a 44-banana tadpole, with class 𝔹4=(𝕋+1)​(𝕋2+2​𝕋−1)​𝕋{\mathbb{B}}_{4}=({\mathbb{T}}+1)({\mathbb{T}}^{2}+2{\mathbb{T}}-1){\mathbb{T}}, and of a melonic part which may be constructed by

(((4),0,1),((1,3,1),1,1))\big(((4),0,1),((1,3,1),1,1)\big)

i.e., by the labeled tree

The recursion obtained above computes the Grothendieck class of this melonic graph to be

𝕋2​(𝕋+1)4​(𝕋2+3​𝕋−2).{\mathbb{T}}^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}({\mathbb{T}}^{2}+3{\mathbb{T}}-2)\quad.

The conclusion is that the Grothendieck class for the graph in Figure 2 equals

𝕋3(𝕋+1)7(𝕋2+3𝕋−2)(𝕋2+2𝕋−1)=(𝕊+1)3(𝕊+2)5(𝕊2+4𝕊+2)(𝕊2+5𝕊+2):{\mathbb{T}}^{3}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{7}({\mathbb{T}}^{2}+3{\mathbb{T}}-2)({\mathbb{T}}^{2}+2{\mathbb{T}}-1)=({\mathbb{S}}+1)^{3}({\mathbb{S}}+2)^{5}({\mathbb{S}}^{2}+4{\mathbb{S}}+2)({\mathbb{S}}^{2}+5{\mathbb{S}}+2)\quad:

indeed, the graph may be obtained by splitting one edge in each of the two components (which has the effect of multiplying each Grothendieck class by 𝕋+1{\mathbb{T}}+1), and then joining the resulting graphs at the newly created vertices, i.e., multiplying together the two resulting Grothendieck classes. ⌟\lrcorner

Positivity as a polynomial in the class 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} is a torification of the Grothendieck class, which may or may not be induced by a geometric torification of the underlying variety, see [26]. The presence of a torified Grothendieck class has consequences in terms of “geometry over the field with one element”, [8], [26]. One can similarly ask whether the positivity of the Grothendieck class as a function of 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} is induced by an underlying geometric structure and whether such a structure carries arithmetic significance. For example, the Grothendieck class of the moduli spaces ℳ0,n\mathcal{M}_{0,n} of genus zero curves with marked points have the simple expression

[ℳ0,n]=(𝕊n−3)⁡(n−3)![{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}]=\binom{{\mathbb{S}}}{n-3}(n-3)!

in terms of the class 𝕊{\mathbb{S}}, with [ℳ0,4]=𝕊[\mathcal{M}_{0,4}]={\mathbb{S}}. However, these classes are not positive in 𝕊{\mathbb{S}}, while the classes of the ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n} moduli spaces satisfy positivity (both in 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} and in 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}), see [26].

Another feature of the polynomials expressing the classes in terms of 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} appears to be the following.

Conjecture 3.1.

Let GG be a melonic graph, and let 𝕌⁡(G)=a0+a1​𝕊+⋯+an​𝕊n{\mathbb{U}}(G)=a_{0}+a_{1}{\mathbb{S}}+\cdots+a_{n}{\mathbb{S}}^{n} be its Grothendieck class. Then the sequence a0,a1,…,ana_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{n} is log concave, i.e., ai−1​ai+1≤ai2a_{i-1}a_{i+1}\leq a_{i}^{2} for 0<i<n0<i<n.

We have verified this conjecture for all melonic graphs with ≤13\leq 13 edges and for hundreds of individual examples from the families of melonic graphs considered in this paper.

One may verify that all these polynomials are log-concave (in the sense that the coefficients of their expansions are log-concave sequences). The number of distinct Grothendieck classes for melonic graphs with nn edges is

1,2,2,4,6,11,18,33,59,114,220,454,954​…1,2,2,4,6,11,18,33,59,114,220,454,954\dots

respectively as n=1,2,3,…n=1,2,3,\dots ⌟\lrcorner

The log-concavity property of the Grothendieck classes implies similar properties for the image of these classes under any motivic measure, meaning a ring homomorphism μ:K0​(𝒱)→R\mu:K_{0}({\mathcal{V}})\to R. Such measures include the topological Euler characteristic and the Hodge–Deligne polynomials (for complex varieties) or the counting of points (for varieties over finite fields). As discussed in [24], the presence of a log-concave structure is usually a sign of the presence of an underlying richer kind of structure, in the form of Hodge-de Rham relations. These can be seen as a broad combinatorial generalization of the setting of the Grothendieck standard conjectures for algebraic cycles. Such combinatorial Hodge-de Rham relations arise, for example, in the context of the log-concavity property of characteristic polynomial of matroids, [1]. Thus, the observed log-concavity of the Grothendieck classes of the graph hypersurface complements as a function of the 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} variable suggest the presence of a more interesting underlying geometric structure in this Hodge-de Rham sense.

While the Grothendieck classes are positive in the class 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} and display this intriguing property, we will persist in using 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} in most of the examples that follow, since the coefficients of the powers of 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} in these classes tend to be smaller.

4. Explicit computations, I

The recursion obtained in §3 is easily implemented in any symbolic manipulation package, and this makes it possible to explore the landscape of Grothendieck classes for natural families of melonic graphs. We will present a selection of such formulas in the sections that follow. While we are able to prove these formulas (see §7), the recursion formulas were key to discovering them, and often the numerical evidence we gathered was quite sufficient to convince us of their truth. It would be worthwhile studying other natural families of melonic graphs using the same method.

In this section we focus on melonic graph with internal vertices of valence 44, and we will use the shorthand for such graphs introduced in §2.

Example 4.1.

For a simple valence-44 example that can be computed without employing the full recursion from §3, we can consider the graph

with nn circles. A corresponding melonic construction is (0,1−,2−,3−,…,(n−1)−)(0,1^{-},2^{-},3^{-},\dots,(n-1)^{-}). This construction is non-reduced; a reduced alternative is simply the 11-stage construction

((1,3,1,3,1,3,…,1),0,1).((1,3,1,3,1,3,\dots,1),0,1)\quad.

The corresponding Grothendieck class is a product of classes of 33-bananas and (𝕋+1)({\mathbb{T}}+1)-factors, accounting for the external and internal single edges. Explicitly, the class equals

𝔹3n⋅(𝕋+1)n+1=𝕋n​(𝕋+1)3​n+1.{\mathbb{B}}_{3}^{n}\cdot({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{n+1}={\mathbb{T}}^{n}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{3n+1}\quad.

for nn circles. ⌟\lrcorner

4.2. Relations of vacuum and non-vacuum graphs

A particularly careful reader may notice the following relation from the data shown above:

(4.3) An′​(t)=An​(t)−An−1​(t).A^{\prime}_{n}(t)=A_{n}(t)-A_{n-1}(t)\quad.

This relation is not a coincidence; it follows from a general formula relating Grothendieck classes of melonic vacuum graphs to classes of related non-vacuum graphs. We will prove this formula in §6.

An even more careful reader may guess the divisibility relation

(4.4) 𝕌(Γn)|𝕌(Γ2​n+1′):{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{n})\,|\,{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{\prime}_{2n+1})\quad:

for example,

A7′​(t)=(t2+5​t+2)​(t2+2​t−2)⋅A3​(t).A^{\prime}_{7}(t)=(t^{2}+5t+2)(t^{2}+2t-2)\cdot A_{3}(t)\quad.

The relation (4.4) will also be obtained as a corollary of a more general result on melonic vacuum graphs, Proposition 6.3 in §6 (see Remark 6.1). ⌟\lrcorner

More examples of computations of Grothendieck classes for melonic vacuum graphs will be given in §6.

The proofs we will discuss in §7 will clarify the presence of the factors 𝕋i​(𝕋+1)j{\mathbb{T}}^{i}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{j} in the Grothendieck classes for the valence-44 graphs considered in this section. The example (0,1+,1+,1+)(0,1^{+},1^{+},1^{+}),

with Grothendieck class

shows that 𝕋n​(𝕋+1)2​n+1{\mathbb{T}}^{n}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2n+1} is not a common factor of the Grothendieck classes of all nn-stage valence-44 melonic constructions.

5. Explicit computations, II

5.1. Rational generating functions for Γn\Gamma_{n} graphs

While §4 and §6 focus on valence-44 graphs, the same types of computation can be carried out for melonic graphs of any fixed valence for internal vertices. In order to obtain simpler statements, it is helpful to express the results stated in Examples 4.2 and 4.3 in terms of rational generating functions.

Proposition 5.1.

With notation as in Examples 4.2 and 4.3, and setting A0​(t)=A0′​(t)=1A_{0}(t)=A^{\prime}_{0}(t)=1,

∑n≥0An​(t)​rn\displaystyle\sum_{n\geq 0}A_{n}(t)r^{n} =1−r1−(2+t)​r+2​r2;\displaystyle=\frac{1-r}{1-(2+t)r+2r^{2}}\quad;
∑n≥0An′​(t)​rn\displaystyle\sum_{n\geq 0}A^{\prime}_{n}(t)r^{n} =(1−r)21−(2+t)​r+2​r2.\displaystyle=\frac{(1-r)^{2}}{1-(2+t)r+2r^{2}}\quad.
Proof.

We verify that the polynomials An​(t)A_{n}(t), An′​(t)A^{\prime}_{n}(t) defined by these expansions agree with those given in Examples 4.2 and 4.3.

Concerning An​(t)A_{n}(t), let τ=(r2−r​t)12\tau=(r^{2}-rt)^{\frac{1}{2}}; then

1−r1−(2+t)​r+2​r2=1−r(1−r−i​τ)​(1−r+i​τ)=12​(11−r−i​τ+11−r+i​τ).\frac{1-r}{1-(2+t)r+2r^{2}}=\frac{1-r}{(1-r-i\tau)(1-r+i\tau)}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{1-r-i\tau}+\frac{1}{1-r+i\tau}\right)\quad.

The terms in the power series expansion of this expression are combinations of powers of (r−i​τ)(r-i\tau) and (r+i​τ)(r+i\tau), so they may be obtained as the coefficients of skk!\frac{s^{k}}{k!} in

12​(e(r+i​τ)​s+e(r−i​τ)​s)=er​s⋅ei​τ​s+e−i​τ​s2=er​s​cos⁡(τ​s).\frac{1}{2}\left(e^{(r+i\tau)s}+e^{(r-i\tau)s}\right)=e^{rs}\cdot\frac{e^{i\tau s}+e^{-i\tau s}}{2}=e^{rs}\cos(\tau s)\quad.

This recovers the description of An​(t)A_{n}(t) given in Proposition 4.1.

The argument for An′​(t)A^{\prime}_{n}(t) is of course analogous. Again setting τ=(r2−r​t)12\tau=(r^{2}-rt)^{\frac{1}{2}}, we have

(1−r)21−(2+t)​r+2​r2\displaystyle\frac{(1-r)^{2}}{1-(2+t)r+2r^{2}} =12​(1−r1−r−i​τ+1−r1−r+i​τ)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1-r}{1-r-i\tau}+\frac{1-r}{1-r+i\tau}\right)
=12​(11−i​τ1−r+11+i​τ1−r)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{1-i\frac{\tau}{1-r}}+\frac{1}{1+i\frac{\tau}{1-r}}\right)

and the terms in the power series expansion of this expression are the coefficients of skk!\frac{s^{k}}{k!} in

12​(ei​τ1−r+e−i​τ1−r)=cos⁡(τ1−r),\frac{1}{2}\left(e^{i\frac{\tau}{1-r}}+e^{-i\frac{\tau}{1-r}}\right)=\cos\left(\frac{\tau}{1-r}\right)\quad,

recovering the description of An′​(t)A^{\prime}_{n}(t) in Proposition 4.3. ∎

6. Vacua

In this section we focus on melonic vacuum graphs. We first observe that there is a close relation between Grothendieck classes of vacuum graphs and of related non-vacuum graphs. For this discussion, the graphs are not necessarily assumed to be melonic; however, the result will explain melonic relations such as the one observed in (4.3).

6.1. Vacuum and non-vacuum graphs relations

Assume Γv\Gamma^{v} is a graph with a distinguished edge:

and assume this edge is not a bridge in Γv\Gamma^{v}. Consider two associated graphs: the graph Γ\Gamma obtained by cutting the edge, and the graph Γ¯\overline{\Gamma} obtained by inserting a new edge crossing the given edge, with vertices as indicated:

Lemma 6.1.
𝕌⁡(Γv)=𝕌⁡(Γ¯)−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​𝕌​(Γ)𝕋​(𝕋+1)4{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{v})=\frac{{\mathbb{U}}(\overline{\Gamma})-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma)}{{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}}
Proof.

This is an application of the formula for the effect on Grothendieck classes of adding one parallel edge to a given (non-bridge, non-looping) edge in a graph, i.e., the case m=2m=2 of (3.5). Place two valence-22 vertices on the joined edge in Γv\Gamma^{v}, creating an edge ee in a graph Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}; by construction, ee is neither a bridge nor a looping edge. Then

𝕌⁡(Γ′)=(𝕋+1)2​𝕌​(Γv),𝕌⁡(Γ′/e)=(𝕋+1)​𝕌​(Γv),{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{\prime})=({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{v})\quad,\quad{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{\prime}/e)=({\mathbb{T}}+1){\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{v})\quad,

while Γ′∖e=Γ\Gamma^{\prime}\smallsetminus e=\Gamma. Replacing ee by two parallel edges produces Γ¯\overline{\Gamma} without the two external edges. Applying (3.5) then gives

𝕌⁡(Γ¯)(𝕋+1)2=f2​(𝕋+1)2​𝕌​(Γv)+g2​(𝕋+1)​𝕌​(Γv)+h2​𝕌​(Γ),\frac{{\mathbb{U}}(\overline{\Gamma})}{({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}}=f_{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{v})+g_{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1){\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{v})+h_{2}{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma)\quad,

that is (cf. (3.6))

𝕌⁡(Γ¯)(𝕋+1)2=𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​𝕌​(Γv)+𝕋​𝕌​(Γ),\frac{{\mathbb{U}}(\overline{\Gamma})}{({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}}={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{v})+{\mathbb{T}}{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma)\quad,

with the stated result. ∎

In the applications we have in mind, Γ\Gamma may be a melonic non-vacuum graphs constructed by

((1,a2,…,ar−1,1),0,1),t2,…,tn;((1,a_{2},\dots,a_{r-1},1),0,1),t_{2},\dots,t_{n}\quad;

the graph Γv\Gamma^{v} will then be the (melonic) vacuum graph obtained by joining the two valence-11 vertices of Γ\Gamma, and Γ¯\overline{\Gamma} is the non-vacuum graph constructed by

((1,3,1),0,1),((1,a2,…,ar−1,1),1,2),t2′,…,tn′((1,3,1),0,1),((1,a_{2},\dots,a_{r-1},1),1,2),t^{\prime}_{2},\dots,t^{\prime}_{n}

where ti′=(bi,pi+1,ki)t^{\prime}_{i}=(b_{i},p_{i}+1,k_{i}) if ti=(bi,pi,ki)t_{i}=(b_{i},p_{i},k_{i}), i=2,…,ni=2,\dots,n. Lemma 6.1 shows that the class 𝕌⁡(Γv){\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{v}) of the vacuum graph is determined by the classes 𝕌⁡(Γ){\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma), 𝕌⁡(Γ¯){\mathbb{U}}(\overline{\Gamma}) of the associated non-vacuum graphs.

For example, with notation as in §4, Lemma 6.1 implies that

𝕌⁡(Γn+1′)=𝕌⁡(Γn+1)−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​𝕌​(Γn)𝕋​(𝕋+1)4;{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{\prime}_{n+1})=\frac{{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{n+1})-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{n})}{{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}}\quad;

with 𝕌⁡(Γn)=𝕋n​(𝕋+1)2​n+1​An​(𝕋){\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{n})={\mathbb{T}}^{n}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2n+1}A_{n}({\mathbb{T}}) and 𝕌⁡(Γn′)=𝕋n−1​(𝕋+1)2​n−3​An′​(𝕋){\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{\prime}_{n})={\mathbb{T}}^{n-1}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2n-3}A^{\prime}_{n}({\mathbb{T}}) as in §4, this relation gives

𝕋n​(𝕋+1)2​n−1​An+1′​(𝕋)=𝕋n+1​(𝕋+1)2​n+3​An+1​(𝕋)−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​𝕋n​(𝕋+1)2​n+1​An​(𝕋)𝕋​(𝕋+1)4,{\mathbb{T}}^{n}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2n-1}A^{\prime}_{n+1}({\mathbb{T}})=\frac{{\mathbb{T}}^{n+1}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2n+3}A_{n+1}({\mathbb{T}})-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}{\mathbb{T}}^{n}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2n+1}A_{n}({\mathbb{T}})}{{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}},

that is,

and this proves (4.3).

6.2. Tree structure for valence-four vacua

Next, we consider specifically melonic vacuum graphs in which every vertex has valence 44. These graphs may be drawn as loopless unions of ovals:

The information carried by a vacuum melonic graph in valence 44 is equivalent to the information of a tree, for example the tree

for the graph shown above. Every node of this tree corresponds to one of the ovals, and two nodes are connected by an edge if and only if the corresponding ovals meet. Given a tree, a corresponding melonic construction is obtained in the evident way by associating one arbitrary edge of the tree with a 44-banana and labeling the other edges with appropriate ((1,3,1),∗,∗)((1,3,1),*,*) tuples as prescribed by adjacencies in the tree. For example, the edges of the above tree could be marked as follows (where we also numbered the edge of the tree to reflect the stage of the corresponding tuple in the melonic construction; many other choices are possible):

leading to the melonic construction

(6.1) ((4),0,1),((1,3,1),1,1),((1,3,1),2,1),((1,3,1),1,1),((1,3,1),4,2),((1,3,1),5,1),((1,3,1),6,2).((4),0,1),((1,3,1),1,1),((1,3,1),2,1),((1,3,1),1,1),\\ ((1,3,1),4,2),((1,3,1),5,1),((1,3,1),6,2)\quad.

Alternatively, one could label one node of the tree by a 22-banana and the remaining nodes by ((1,3,1),∗,∗)((1,3,1),*,*) tuples; the corresponding construction will produce a vacuum melonic graph with two extra valence-22 vertices. This strategy is used below in Example 6.1.

6.3. Recursion relations for vacuum bubbles

It is natural to ask whether a simple recursion may exist between the Grothendieck classes of vacuum melonic graphs, reflecting the tree-like structure underlying them. The only instance known to us of such a recursion goes as follows. Assume a branch of the tree projects out of the main body; let UnU_{n} denote the Grothendieck class of the vacuum melonic graph obtained by adding nn edges to such a branch.

Claim 6.2.

For n≥2n\geq 2,

(6.2) Un+1=𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​(𝕋+2)​Un−2​𝕋2​(𝕋+1)4​Un−1.U_{n+1}={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,U_{n}-2{\mathbb{T}}^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}\,U_{n-1}\quad.

We will prove this formula in §7; in fact we will prove that this formula holds even if the starting graph is not melonic. This will be our main tool in the proofs of the propositions stated thus far, as well as Proposition 6.3, stated below.

If s≤2​ns\leq 2n, then 𝕌​(Γn)s−1{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{n})^{s-1} divides 𝕌⁡(Σns){\mathbb{U}}(\Sigma^{s}_{n}). More precisely,

Proof.

Remark 6.1.

Corollary 6.4 implies the divisibility relation (4.4) observed in §4. Indeed, the graph Σn2\Sigma^{2}_{n} consists of a string of 2​n+12n+1 circles:

That is, Σn2=Γ2​n+1′\Sigma^{2}_{n}=\Gamma^{\prime}_{2n+1}, with notation as in Example 4.3. For this graph, Corollary 6.4 states that 𝕌⁡(Γn){\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{n}) divides 𝕌⁡(Γ2​n+1′){\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{\prime}_{2n+1}), and this is precisely the assertion in (4.4). ⌟\lrcorner

7. Proofs

Proposition 4.1 and Proposition 4.3 will be proved in the equivalent form presented in Proposition 5.1. For clarity we will focus on the case of valence 44 given in these propositions; the same method could be used to prove Proposition 5.3.

The statement we will prove will actually be substantially more general than Propositions 4.1 and 4.3: it consists of a recursion ruling the Grothendieck classes of graphs obtained by extending any given graph by a tower of 33-bananas.

Let GG be a (not necessarily melonic) graph, and let ee be an edge of GG. Let GnG_{n} be the graph obtained by applying a chain of (1,3,1)(1,3,1)-bananifications starting from ee:

Theorem 7.1.

The generating function for the Grothendieck classes 𝕌⁡(Gn){\mathbb{U}}(G_{n}) is rational, with denominator independent of GG. More precisely, there exists a polynomial P⁡(𝕋,ρ)P({\mathbb{T}},\rho) with integer coefficients such that

∑n≥0𝕌⁡(Gn)​ρn=P⁡(𝕋,ρ)1−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​(𝕋+2)​ρ+2​𝕋2​(𝕋+1)4​ρ2\sum_{n\geq 0}{\mathbb{U}}(G_{n})\rho^{n}=\frac{P({\mathbb{T}},\rho)}{1-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,\rho+2{\mathbb{T}}^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}\,\rho^{2}}

This statement focuses on the fact that the generating function is rational, and gives an explicit form for its denominator, which depends on the bananification process itself rather than on the graph GG. The graph GG determines the numerator P⁡(𝕋,ρ)P({\mathbb{T}},\rho); precise formulas will be given below in Theorem 7.2. In practice, Theorem 7.1 and a few case-by-case explicit computations of 𝕌⁡(Gn){\mathbb{U}}(G_{n}) for low values of nn determine P⁡(𝕋,ρ)P({\mathbb{T}},\rho).

Proof.

Denote by HnH_{n} the graph obtained from GnG_{n} by replacing the last 33-bananification with a 22-bananification:

Denote 𝕌⁡(Gn){\mathbb{U}}(G_{n}) by UnU_{n}, 𝕌⁡(Hn){\mathbb{U}}(H_{n}) by VnV_{n}. Assume n≥2n\geq 2. Consider the graph G′′G^{\prime\prime} obtained by splitting one of the parallel edges of the top banana in Gn−1G_{n-1} into three edges; let e′e^{\prime} be the central edge so produced, and note that e′e^{\prime} is not a bridge or a looping edge of G′′G^{\prime\prime}.

The contraction G′:=G′′/e′G^{\prime}:=G^{\prime\prime}/e^{\prime} may be obtained from Gn−1G_{n-1} by splitting the same edge of the top banana into two edges, and the deletion H′=G′′∖e′H^{\prime}=G^{\prime\prime}\smallsetminus e^{\prime} may be obtained from Hn−1H_{n-1} by attaching two external edges to the vertices of the top (22-)banana:

By (3.5), we have

Vn\displaystyle V_{n} =f2​𝕌​(G′′)+g2​𝕌​(G′)+h2​𝕌​(H′)\displaystyle=f_{2}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G^{\prime\prime})+g_{2}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G^{\prime})+h_{2}\,{\mathbb{U}}(H^{\prime})
Un\displaystyle U_{n} =f3​𝕌​(G′′)+g3​𝕌​(G′)+h3​𝕌​(H′),\displaystyle=f_{3}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G^{\prime\prime})+g_{3}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G^{\prime})+h_{3}\,{\mathbb{U}}(H^{\prime})\quad,

where f2,f3f_{2},f_{3}, etc., are as in (3.6). We now note that

{𝕌⁡(G′′)=(𝕋+1)2​𝕌​(Gn−1)=(𝕋+1)2​Un−1𝕌⁡(G′)=(𝕋+1)​𝕌​(Gn−1)=(𝕋+1)​Un−1𝕌⁡(H′)=(𝕋+1)2​𝕌​(Hn−1)=(𝕋+1)2​Vn−1;\left\{\begin{aligned} {\mathbb{U}}(G^{\prime\prime})&=({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}{\mathbb{U}}(G_{n-1})=({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}U_{n-1}\\ {\mathbb{U}}(G^{\prime})&=({\mathbb{T}}+1)\,\,{\mathbb{U}}(G_{n-1})=({\mathbb{T}}+1)\,\,U_{n-1}\\ {\mathbb{U}}(H^{\prime})&=({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}{\mathbb{U}}(H_{n-1})=({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}V_{n-1}\end{aligned}\right.\quad;

further,

f2​(𝕋+1)2+g2​(𝕋+1)=𝕋​(𝕋+1)2,f3​(𝕋+1)2+g3​(𝕋+1)=𝕋​(𝕋+1)3f_{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}+g_{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1)={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\quad,\quad f_{3}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}+g_{3}({\mathbb{T}}+1)={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{3}

while h2=𝕋h_{2}={\mathbb{T}}, h3=(𝕋−1)​𝕋h_{3}=({\mathbb{T}}-1){\mathbb{T}}. The above formulas can then be rewritten

(7.1) Vn\displaystyle V_{n} =𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​Un−1+𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​Vn−1\displaystyle={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,U_{n-1}+{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,V_{n-1}

These imply

(𝕋−1)​Vn\displaystyle({\mathbb{T}}-1)V_{n} =(𝕋−1)​𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​Un−1+(𝕋−1)​𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​Vn−1\displaystyle=({\mathbb{T}}-1){\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,U_{n-1}+({\mathbb{T}}-1){\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,V_{n-1}
=(𝕋−1)​𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​Un−1+(Un−𝕋​(𝕋+1)3​Un−1)\displaystyle=({\mathbb{T}}-1){\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,U_{n-1}+\big(U_{n}-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{3}\,U_{n-1}\big)
=Un−2​𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​Un−1\displaystyle=U_{n}-2{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,U_{n-1}

and therefore

=𝕋​(𝕋+1)3​Un+𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​(Un−2​𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​Un−1)\displaystyle={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{3}\,U_{n}+{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,\left(U_{n}-2{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,U_{n-1}\right)
=𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​(𝕋+2)​Un−2​𝕋2​(𝕋+1)4​Un−1.\displaystyle={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,U_{n}-2{\mathbb{T}}^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}\,U_{n-1}\quad.

(This proves Claim 6.2.) Now, for n≥2n\geq 2, the coefficient of ρn+1\rho^{n+1} in the product

equals

This product is therefore a polynomial P⁡(𝕋,ρ)P({\mathbb{T}},\rho), and this proves the statement. ∎

The argument shows that

(7.2) P⁡(𝕋,ρ)\displaystyle P({\mathbb{T}},\rho) =(1−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​(𝕋+2)​ρ+2​𝕋2​(𝕋+1)4​ρ2)⋅∑n≥0Un​ρn\displaystyle=\big(1-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,\rho+2{\mathbb{T}}^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}\,\rho^{2}\big)\cdot\sum_{n\geq 0}U_{n}\,\rho^{n}
=𝕌⁡(G)+(𝕌⁡(G1)−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​(𝕋+2)​𝕌​(G))​ρ\displaystyle={\mathbb{U}}(G)+({\mathbb{U}}(G_{1})-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,{\mathbb{U}}(G))\,\rho
+(𝕌⁡(G2)−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​(𝕋+2)​𝕌​(G1)+2​𝕋2​(𝕋+1)4​𝕌​(G))​ρ2.\displaystyle+\big({\mathbb{U}}(G_{2})-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,{\mathbb{U}}(G_{1})+2{\mathbb{T}}^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G)\big)\,\rho^{2}\quad.

If ee is not a bridge, then the argument proves the same recursion for n≥1n\geq 1; it follows that the coefficient of ρ2\rho^{2} in P⁡(𝕋,ρ)P({\mathbb{T}},\rho) is 00 in this case. Maybe a little surprisingly, the same conclusion holds if ee is a bridge (as we will prove below); thus, the polynomial P⁡(𝕋,ρ)P({\mathbb{T}},\rho) is of degree 11 in ρ\rho. This polynomial is determined by 𝕌⁡(G){\mathbb{U}}(G) and the deletion 𝕌⁡(G∖e){\mathbb{U}}(G\smallsetminus e), as we will see below.

In fact, Theorem 7.1 and the direct computation of a few values of 𝕌⁡(Gn){\mathbb{U}}(G_{n}) suffice to determine the numerator.

Example 7.1.

The melonic valence-44 vacuum graphs corresponding to the trees

((4),0,1),((1,3,1),1,1),((1,3,1),2,1),((1,3,1),1,1),((1,3,1),4,2),((1,3,1),5,1),((1,3,1),6,2),((1,3,1),6,1),((1,3,1),8,2),…,((1,3,1),n+6,2).((4),0,1),((1,3,1),1,1),((1,3,1),2,1),((1,3,1),1,1),\\ ((1,3,1),4,2),((1,3,1),5,1),((1,3,1),6,2),\\ ((1,3,1),6,1),((1,3,1),8,2),\dots,((1,3,1),n+6,2)\quad.

In general, P⁡(𝕋,ρ)P({\mathbb{T}},\rho) is determined by the Grothendieck classes of GG and (if ee is not a bridge) G∖eG\smallsetminus e, if the latter is known.

Theorem 7.2.

With notation as above, let r=𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​ρr={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,\rho. Then we have

∑n≥0𝕌⁡(Gn)​ρn=1−r1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2⋅𝕌⁡(G)\sum_{n\geq 0}{\mathbb{U}}(G_{n})\rho^{n}=\frac{1-r}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}\cdot{\mathbb{U}}(G)

if ee is a bridge in GG, and

∑n≥0𝕌⁡(Gn)​ρn=𝕌⁡(G)+((𝕋−1)​𝕌​(G∖e)−𝕌⁡(G))​r1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2\sum_{n\geq 0}{\mathbb{U}}(G_{n})\,\rho^{n}=\frac{{\mathbb{U}}(G)+\big(({\mathbb{T}}-1)\,{\mathbb{U}}(G\smallsetminus e)-{\mathbb{U}}(G)\big)\,r}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}

if ee is not a bridge in GG.

Proof.

The argument proving Theorem 7.1 shows that the coefficient of ρn\rho^{n} in P⁡(𝕋,ρ)P({\mathbb{T}},\rho) is 00 for n≥3n\geq 3, and for n≥2n\geq 2 if ee is not a bridge, as observed above. If ee is a bridge,

U1=(T+1)2​𝔹​(3)​𝕌​(G∖e)=𝕋​(𝕋+1)4​𝕌​(G∖e)=𝕋​(𝕋+1)3​U0,U_{1}=(T+1)^{2}\,{\mathbb{B}}(3)\,{\mathbb{U}}(G\smallsetminus e)={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G\smallsetminus e)={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{3}\,U_{0}\quad,

since G1G_{1} is obtained by replacing the central split of ee, a bridge, with a 33-banana. By the same token,

V1=(T+1)2​𝔹​(2)​𝕌​(G∖e)=𝕋​(𝕋+1)3​𝕌​(G∖e)=𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​U0.V_{1}=(T+1)^{2}\,{\mathbb{B}}(2)\,{\mathbb{U}}(G\smallsetminus e)={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{3}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G\smallsetminus e)={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,U_{0}\quad.

By (7.1) we have

U2\displaystyle U_{2} =𝕋​(𝕋+1)3​U1+(𝕋−1)​𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​V1\displaystyle={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{3}\,U_{1}+({\mathbb{T}}-1){\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,V_{1}
=𝕋3​(𝕋+1)4​(𝕋+3)​U0.\displaystyle={\mathbb{T}}^{3}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}({\mathbb{T}}+3)\,U_{0}\quad.

On the other hand,

𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​(𝕋+2)​U1−2​𝕋2​(𝕋+1)4​U0\displaystyle{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,U_{1}-2\,{\mathbb{T}}^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}\,U_{0} =𝕋2​(𝕋+1)5​(𝕋+2)​U0−2​𝕋2​(𝕋+1)4​U0\displaystyle={\mathbb{T}}^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{5}({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,U_{0}-2\,{\mathbb{T}}^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}\,U_{0}
=𝕋3​(𝕋+1)4​(𝕋+3)​U0.\displaystyle={\mathbb{T}}^{3}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{4}({\mathbb{T}}+3)\,U_{0}\quad.

This verifies that the coefficient of ρ2\rho^{2} in P⁡(𝕋,ρ)P({\mathbb{T}},\rho) (see (7.2)) equals 00 in this case as well. Therefore, in all cases we have

P⁡(𝕋,ρ)=𝕌⁡(G)+(𝕌⁡(G1)−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​(𝕋+2)​𝕌​(G))​ρ.P({\mathbb{T}},\rho)={\mathbb{U}}(G)+({\mathbb{U}}(G_{1})-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,{\mathbb{U}}(G))\,\rho\quad.

If ee is a bridge, the coefficient of ρ\rho in P⁡(𝕋,ρ)P({\mathbb{T}},\rho) is

𝕌⁡(G1)−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​(𝕋+2)​𝕌​(G)=−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​𝕌​(G){\mathbb{U}}(G_{1})-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,{\mathbb{U}}(G)=-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G)

since 𝕌⁡(G1)=U1=𝕋​(𝕋+1)3​U0=𝕋​(𝕋+1)3​𝕌​(G){\mathbb{U}}(G_{1})=U_{1}={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{3}\,U_{0}={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{3}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G) as we observed above. Therefore

P⁡(𝕋,ρ)=𝕌⁡(G)−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​𝕌​(G)​ρ=(1−r)​𝕌​(G)P({\mathbb{T}},\rho)={\mathbb{U}}(G)-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G)\rho=(1-r)\,{\mathbb{U}}(G)

if ee is a bridge, and this gives the first formula.

If ee is not a bridge, splitting it into three and 33-bananifying the central edge gives, arguing as in the proof of Theorem 7.1,

𝕌⁡(G1)=𝕋​(𝕋+1)3​𝕌​(G)+(𝕋−1)​𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​𝕌​(G∖e){\mathbb{U}}(G_{1})={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{3}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G)+({\mathbb{T}}-1){\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G\smallsetminus e)

and therefore

𝕌⁡(G1)−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​(𝕋+2)​𝕌​(G)=−𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​𝕌​(G)+(𝕋−1)​𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​𝕌​(G∖e).{\mathbb{U}}(G_{1})-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,{\mathbb{U}}(G)=-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G)+({\mathbb{T}}-1){\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,{\mathbb{U}}(G\smallsetminus e)\quad.

It follows that the degree-11 term in P⁡(𝕋,ρ)P({\mathbb{T}},\rho) in this case is

(−𝕌⁡(G)+(𝕋−1)​𝕌​(G∖e))​𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​ρ,(-{\mathbb{U}}(G)+({\mathbb{T}}-1)\,{\mathbb{U}}(G\smallsetminus e))\,{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\,\rho\quad,

and this completes the proof of the second formula. ∎

The fact that the formulas in Theorem 7.2 depend on r=𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​ρr={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\rho explains why the specific examples worked out in Propositions 4.1 and 4.3 included powers of 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} and 𝕋+1{\mathbb{T}}+1 as stated. We recover these results in the next two examples.

Example 7.2.

Define the polynomials An​(t)A_{n}(t) by the power series expansion

𝕌⁡(Γn)=𝕋n​(𝕋+1)2​n+1​An​(𝕋),{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{n})={\mathbb{T}}^{n}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2n+1}A_{n}({\mathbb{T}})\quad,

proving Proposition 4.1 (in the form given in Proposition 5.1). ⌟\lrcorner

Example 7.3.

Now let GG be a 22-banana, and let ee be one of its (two) edges. The graph G∖eG\smallsetminus e is a single edge. Therefore

𝕌⁡(G)=𝕋⁡(𝕋+1),𝕌⁡(G∖e)=𝕋+1,{\mathbb{U}}(G)={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)\quad,\quad{\mathbb{U}}(G\smallsetminus e)={\mathbb{T}}+1\quad,

and the second formula in Theorem 7.2 states that

∑n≠0𝕌⁡(Gn)​ρn\displaystyle\sum_{n\neq 0}{\mathbb{U}}(G_{n})\,\rho^{n} =𝕋⁡(𝕋+1)+((𝕋−1)​(𝕋+1)−𝕋⁡(𝕋+1))​r1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2\displaystyle=\frac{{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)+\big(({\mathbb{T}}-1)({\mathbb{T}}+1)-{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)\big)r}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}
=(𝕋−r)1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2⋅(𝕋+1)\displaystyle=\frac{\big({\mathbb{T}}-r\big)}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}\cdot({\mathbb{T}}+1)

With notation as in §4, the graph GnG_{n} (consisting of a chain of n+1n+1 circles) equals Γn+1′\Gamma^{\prime}_{n+1}, with two extra valence-22 vertices on the first circle. That is,

𝕌⁡(Γn′)=𝕌⁡(Gn−1)(𝕋+1)2.{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{\prime}_{n})=\frac{{\mathbb{U}}(G_{n-1})}{({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}}\quad.

Now, since r=𝕋​(𝕋+1)2​ρr={\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}\rho,

𝕌⁡(Gn−1)=𝕋n−1​(𝕋+1)2​n−2⋅coeff. of rn−1 in the expansion of ​(𝕋−r)​(𝕋+1)1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2{\mathbb{U}}(G_{n-1})={\mathbb{T}}^{n-1}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2n-2}\cdot\text{coeff.~of $r^{n-1}$ in the expansion of }\frac{\big({\mathbb{T}}-r\big)({\mathbb{T}}+1)}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}

hence

𝕌⁡(Gn−1)(𝕋+1)2=𝕋n−1​(𝕋+1)2​n−3⋅coeff. of rn−1 in the expansion of ​(𝕋−r)1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2\frac{{\mathbb{U}}(G_{n-1})}{({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2}}={\mathbb{T}}^{n-1}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2n-3}\cdot\text{coeff.~of $r^{n-1}$ in the expansion of }\frac{\big({\mathbb{T}}-r\big)}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}

and therefore

𝕌⁡(Γn′)=𝕋n−1​(𝕋+1)2​n−3⋅coeff. of rn in the expansion of ​r⁡(𝕋−r)1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2.{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma^{\prime}_{n})={\mathbb{T}}^{n-1}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2n-3}\cdot\text{coeff.~of $r^{n}$ in the expansion of }\frac{r\big({\mathbb{T}}-r\big)}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}\quad.

This holds for n≥1n\geq 1; setting (as in §4) the constant term of the relevant series to 11 amounts to adding 11 to this rational function, and

1+r⁡(𝕋−r)1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2=(1−r)21−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r21+\frac{r\big({\mathbb{T}}-r\big)}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}=\frac{(1-r)^{2}}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}

verifying Proposition 4.3, in the form given in Proposition 5.1. ⌟\lrcorner

Example 7.4.

As a final example, we will prove Proposition 6.3, by induction on the number ss of rays. For s=1s=1, the statement reproduces Proposition 4.3; so we only need to prove the induction step, and we may assume s>1s>1.

To transition from Σns−1\Sigma^{s-1}_{n} to Σns\Sigma^{s}_{n}, view Σns\Sigma^{s}_{n} as the graph obtained by adding a chain of 33-bananas to one of the edges ee of the central circle in G=Σns−1G=\Sigma^{s-1}_{n}.

Since ee is not a bridge, we can apply the second formula given in Theorem 7.2. We write it as follows:

1−r1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2​𝕌​(Σns−1)+r⁡(𝕋−1)1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2​𝕌​(Σns−1∖e).\frac{1-r}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}\,{\mathbb{U}}(\Sigma^{s-1}_{n})+\frac{r\,({\mathbb{T}}-1)}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}\,{\mathbb{U}}(\Sigma^{s-1}_{n}\smallsetminus e)\quad.

The class 𝕌⁡(Σns){\mathbb{U}}(\Sigma^{s}_{n}) is the coefficient of ρn\rho^{n} in this expression (i.e., 𝕋n​(𝕋+1)2​n{\mathbb{T}}^{n}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2n} times the coefficient of rnr^{n}). We will deal with the two summands separately.

  • •

    By induction, the first summand equals

    𝕌⁡(Γn)(𝕋+1)⋅𝕋(s−1)​n​(𝕋+1)2​(s−1)​n−1​An​(𝕋)s−2⋅coeff. of rn+1 in ​1−2​r+((s−2)​𝕋−(s−3))​r21−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2\frac{{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{n})}{({\mathbb{T}}+1)}\cdot{\mathbb{T}}^{(s-1)n}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2(s-1)n-1}A_{n}({\mathbb{T}})^{s-2}\cdot\text{coeff.~of $r^{n+1}$ in }\frac{1-2r+((s-2){\mathbb{T}}-(s-3))r^{2}}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)r+2r^{2}}

    and 𝕌⁡(Γn)=𝕋n​(𝕋+1)2​n+1​An​(𝕋){\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{n})={\mathbb{T}}^{n}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2n+1}A_{n}({\mathbb{T}}), so this equals

    𝕋s​n​(𝕋+1)2​s​n−1​An​(𝕋)s−1⋅coeff. of rn+1 in ​1−2​r+((s−2)​𝕋−(s−3))​r21−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2.{\mathbb{T}}^{sn}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2sn-1}A_{n}({\mathbb{T}})^{s-1}\cdot\text{coeff.~of $r^{n+1}$ in }\frac{1-2r+((s-2){\mathbb{T}}-(s-3))r^{2}}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)r+2r^{2}}\quad.
  • •

    In the second summand, Σns−1∖e\Sigma^{s-1}_{n}\smallsetminus e consists of a join of s−1s-1 chains of nn-circles, therefore its Grothendieck class 𝕌⁡(Σns−1∖e){\mathbb{U}}(\Sigma^{s-1}_{n}\smallsetminus e) is the (s−1)(s-1)-st power of 𝕌⁡(Γn){\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{n}), up to an appropriate factor of (𝕋+1)({\mathbb{T}}+1) to account for the fact that Σns−1∖e\Sigma^{s-1}_{n}\smallsetminus e has no valence-22 vertices and no external edges. For example, here is a picture contrasting the join of 33 graphs Γ4\Gamma_{4} (on the left) with Σ43∖e\Sigma^{3}_{4}\smallsetminus e (on the right):

    It follows that

    𝕌⁡(Σns−1∖e)=𝕌​(Γn)s−1(𝕋+1)s=𝕋(s−1)​n​(𝕋+1)2​(s−1)​n−1​An​(𝕋)s−1.{\mathbb{U}}(\Sigma^{s-1}_{n}\smallsetminus e)=\frac{{\mathbb{U}}(\Gamma_{n})^{s-1}}{({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{s}}={\mathbb{T}}^{(s-1)n}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2(s-1)n-1}A_{n}({\mathbb{T}})^{s-1}\quad.

    Therefore, the second summand equals

    𝕋(s−1)​n​(𝕋+1)2​(s−1)​n−1​An​(𝕋)s−1⋅coeff. of ρn in ​r⁡(𝕋−1)1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2.{\mathbb{T}}^{(s-1)n}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2(s-1)n-1}A_{n}({\mathbb{T}})^{s-1}\cdot\text{coeff.~of $\rho^{n}$ in }\frac{r\,({\mathbb{T}}-1)}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}\quad.

    Now, the coefficient of ρn\rho^{n} equals 𝕋​(𝕋+1)2{\mathbb{T}}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2} times the coefficient of rnr^{n}, so this may be rewritten as

    𝕋s​n​(𝕋+1)2​s​n−1​An​(𝕋)s−1⋅coeff. of rn in ​r⁡(𝕋−1)1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2{\mathbb{T}}^{sn}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2sn-1}A_{n}({\mathbb{T}})^{s-1}\cdot\text{coeff.~of $r^{n}$ in }\frac{r\,({\mathbb{T}}-1)}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}

    or equivalently

    𝕋s​n​(𝕋+1)2​s​n−1​An​(𝕋)s−1⋅coeff. of rn+1 in ​r2​(𝕋−1)1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2.{\mathbb{T}}^{sn}({\mathbb{T}}+1)^{2sn-1}A_{n}({\mathbb{T}})^{s-1}\cdot\text{coeff.~of $r^{n+1}$ in }\frac{r^{2}\,({\mathbb{T}}-1)}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}\quad.

1−2​r+((s−2)​𝕋−(s−3))​r21−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2+r2​(𝕋−1)1−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2=1−2​r+((s−1)​𝕋−(s−2))​r21−(𝕋+2)​r+2​r2\frac{1-2r+((s-2){\mathbb{T}}-(s-3))r^{2}}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)r+2r^{2}}+\frac{r^{2}\,({\mathbb{T}}-1)}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)\,r+2\,r^{2}}=\frac{1-2r+((s-1){\mathbb{T}}-(s-2))r^{2}}{1-({\mathbb{T}}+2)r+2r^{2}}

and this verifies the induction step, concluding the proof of Proposition 6.3. ⌟\lrcorner
